questions.worked_solution:
Given an invertible $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}.
$$

First, we find $|A|$ using a Laplace expansion across the $2$nd row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =|\begin{aligned}7 & 6 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}6 & -3 \\ -5 & 2\end{aligned}|+2(-1)^{2+2}|\begin{aligned}7 & -3 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-1(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}7 & 6 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(12-15)+2(14+15)+(-35-30) \\  & =3+58-65 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
|{A}^{-1}|=\frac{1}{|A|}=-\frac{1}{4}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a+2 & -2 & 2 \\ b+3 & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|=5,$
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a+1 & -2 & 2 \\ b & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a+1 & -2 & 2 \\ b & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}(a+2)-1 & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3)-3 & 4 & 2 \\ c+0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $3$rd row, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}(a+2)-1 & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3)-3 & 4 & 2 \\ c+0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}(a+2) & -2 & 2 \\ (b+3) & 4 & 2 \\ c & 0 & 1\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{5}+|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 2 \\ -3 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5+1\cdot (-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =5+(-10) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the $2$nd row of our determinant is almost equal to the $3$rd row. So, we can rewrite the given determinant, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 103 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Next, using the linearity property of determinants, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144+0 & 158+0 & 102+1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

The first determinant must be zero since it has two identical rows, while the second determinant can be expanded across the $2$nd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 144 & 158 & 102 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 144 & 158 & 102\end{aligned}| & =0+1(-1)^{2+3}|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 144 & 158\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(2\cdot 158-4\cdot 144) \\  & =-(316-576) \\  & =260\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 
$|\begin{aligned}a & b & c \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|=3,$
find 
$|\begin{aligned}a-2 & b & c \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|.$
questions.worked_solution:
We "factor out" the given determinant from the determinant we would like to find:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a-2 & b & c \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}a-2 & b+0 & c+0 \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the linearity property of determinants and expanding the second determinant across the $1$st row, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}a-2 & b+0 & c+0 \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & ={{|\begin{aligned}a & b & c \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}|}_{⏟}}_{3}+|\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3-2(-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}5 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3-2\cdot (5+1) \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$
